deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft (Konzept) of the German introductory remarks Riemann prepared for the public disputation of his doctoral dissertation (Göttingen, December 1851; 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'). The previous page is a note to the Dieterich university printer asking for proof sheets for his opponents. The next page is a cleaner fair-copy version of this same text. There is no computation on the page; the content is conceptual and polemical.

(1) Purpose. To fulfil his present obligation (the disputation), Riemann proposes to single out some points of the dissertation on which 'men of recognised reputation' have stated an opposite view. The fair copy reads 'von Männern von anerkanntem Rufe'.

(2) His definition (dissertation §1). A complex quantity w is a function of a complex quantity z = x + iy if it varies with z so that the difference quotient dw/dz is independent of the value of the differential dz. In modern terms, the limit of (w(z+h) - w(z))/h exists and is independent of the direction of h, i.e. w is complex-differentiable. With w = u + iv and u, v differentiable, writing dz = dx + i dy, independence from dz is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y, u_y = -v_x. [This equivalence is my gloss, but it is exactly Riemann's derivation in §1 of the dissertation.]

(3) First opposing view. One ascribes to a function w of z = x + iy the property that dw/dz is independent of dz, but does not take it as part of the definition. Instead one derives it from the allegedly already proven theorem that, for f(a+b), the derivative with respect to a equals the derivative with respect to b. Applied with a = x and b = iy, that gives ∂f/∂x = (1/i) ∂f/∂y, i.e. f_y = i f_x, which is the complex form of the Cauchy-Riemann equations. [Unpacking mine.] The fair copy continues: this theorem is immediate when a, b and f are real, but in the complex case it already presupposes what is to be proved. So the argument is circular unless f is assumed to be an expression built from analytic operations, which ties back to Riemann's remarks on 'Größenoperationen' on the previous page.

(4) Second opposing view, attributed to Cauchy. Any complex quantity w that varies with z = x + iy in some determinate but entirely arbitrary way is called a function of x + iy, i.e. any map (x,y) ↦ u + iv. Riemann cites Cauchy's statement at the session of the Paris Academy of 31 March [1851], made on the occasion of a report on a memoir of Puiseux. The fair copy adds: 'and further developed in several following lectures'.

(5) Latin passage at the bottom. This is apparently a quotation or draft related to Cauchy's position, or a Latin thesis. Translation: 'But we have declared that if, for the values of the argument in a quite small [region/line], the value of the function is given, then from these the values of the function for the remaining values of the argument already follow.' This is the uniqueness (identity) principle for analytic functions, i.e. the determination of a function through analytic continuation from its values on an arbitrarily small set with an accumulation point (e.g. a small arc or region). This holds for Riemann's functions (differentiable in his sense) but fails for Cauchy's 'arbitrary' functions of x + iy, which is presumably why it is set against view two.
errors: No mathematical errors. The draft is rhetorical. The phrase 'Differential einer Function von a+b' should be 'Differentialquotient', as the fair copy has it.

Riemann's implicit criticism of view one is sound. d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b) is trivial for real differentiable f. For complex b = iy it is exactly the Cauchy-Riemann condition, and so cannot be invoked as a previously proven general theorem without assuming complex differentiability.
The identity statement in the Latin is correct for holomorphic functions on a connected domain. 'A quite small region/line' needs at least a set with an accumulation point; a short arc suffices.

results.what: Definition of a function of a complex variable as one whose derivative dw/dz is independent of dz (direction-independent difference quotient)
results.modern_name: Holomorphic/complex-differentiable function; equivalent to Cauchy-Riemann equations
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1814/1825, CR equations), d'Alembert/Euler; definition as foundation: Riemann 1851 dissertation

results.what: Critique of deriving the CR property from the theorem d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b), which is only immediate in the real case
results.modern_name: Circularity of deducing Cauchy-Riemann equations from formal 'function of x+iy'

results.what: Criticism of Cauchy's 1851 notion (report on Puiseux, CR Acad. Sci. 31 March 1851) of an arbitrary complex quantity depending on x+iy as a 'function'
results.modern_name: Distinction between arbitrary maps C→C and monogenic (analytic) functions

results.what: Values on an arbitrarily small set determine the function everywhere
results.modern_name: Identity theorem / uniqueness of analytic continuation
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy/Weierstrass; stated by Riemann in his 1851 dissertation (§19-20 style remarks)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of Riemann's disputation remarks defending his dissertation's definition of a complex function against Cauchy's 1851 notion. The mathematical content (CR definition, identity principle) is well known as his. The explicit polemic against Cauchy's 31 March 1851 report is of modest historical interest; similar material is known from his Nachlass and the literature on the dissertation.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); z=x+I*y; w=z**2; u,v=re(expand(w)),im(expand(w)); simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y))==0 and simplify(diff(u,y)+diff(v,x))==0
checkable.asserts: z^2 satisfies Cauchy-Riemann, i.e. dw/dz independent of dz

checkable.sympy: x,y,t=symbols('x y t',real=True); w=x-I*y; dw=diff(w,x)*cos(t)+diff(w,y)*sin(t); dz=cos(t)+I*sin(t); simplify(dw/dz)
checkable.asserts: For w = conj(z) the quotient dw/dz = exp(-2it) depends on direction of dz, so it is a 'function' in Cauchy's 1851 sense but not Riemann's
Formal identity d/da f(a+b) = d/db f(a+b), the theorem used in the first opposing view
With a=x, b=iy the identity becomes f_y = i f_x, the complex form of Cauchy-Riemann

transcription_corrections: Line 1 likely begins 'Um meiner jetzigen Obliegenheit zu genügen'; '[-Zweck-]' is a deletion before 'Obliegenheit'.
Line 2: 'einige Punkte daraus hervorzuheben' (the '[?]' after Punkte is 'daraus').

Line 3: 'wo von Männern von anerkanntem Rufe eine entgegengesetzte Auffassung/Überzeugung' – 'Rufe' is the interlinear correction above 'Bedeutung'; 'des Ausdrucks' belongs to the next paragraph ('Definition des Ausdrucks').
'Erstens. Es wird einer Function w [-von z-] x' – the stray 'x' is a deletion; read 'einer Function w einer veränderlichen complexen Größe z = x+yi'.
'der Differential einer Function von a+b' should read 'der Differentialquotient (Diffqut) einer Function von a+b nach a genommen gleich ist dem Differentialquotient nach b'.
'(allgemein zu reden auf bestimmte Art) oder auf ganz beliebige Art' – fair copy has 'aber'.
'und in folgenden Worten ausgesprochen' is more likely 'und in mehreren folgenden Vorträgen weiter ausgeführt' (cf. fair copy).
'der Schrift der Comptes rendus' insertion is doubtful; the line reads 'in der Sitzung der Par. Ak. v. 31 März, bei Gelegenheit eines Berichts über eine Arbeit von Puiseux'.

Latin: the insertion above 'admodum exigua' is illegible (possibly a noun like 'linea'/'regione'); read 'si pro valoribus argumenti in [...] admodum exigua valor est datus functionis, ex his valores functionis pro reliquis valoribus argumenti jam sequi'.
